newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FOREIGN INFLOWS SEEN AIDING S.AFRICA FOREX EASING.
newsitem.headline: FOREIGN INFLOWS SEEN AIDING S.AFRICA FOREX EASING.

text.p: The recent inflow of foreign capital into the country bodes well for the impact of the imminent easing of exchange controls on individuals on July 1, the South African Chamber of Business (Sacob) said on Thursday.

"Recent foreign inflows have helped to provide a buffer of reserves that is likely to contribute to bullntiment towards the rand and the economy," Sacob director for economic policy Ben van Rensburg said.
"Markets have had time to adjust and the business mood is rather phlegmatic as to the possible influence (of the exchange control easing) on the economy," he said.

Presenting the chamber's monthly business confidence index, van Rensburg said foreign capital continued to flow into the country from the partial privatisation of telecommunications utility Telkom in March.
South African bonds and equities also continued to be attractive to foreign investors.
Van Rensburg said that while the business mood remained stable, it was adjusting to new economic realities which pointed towards a soft landing for the economy rather than a recession.
Sacob's business confidence index fell by 0.2 percentage points to 113.8 points in May from 114.0 points the previous month and 116.9 a year ago.
The Reserve Bank's contractionary monetary policy continued to put a dampener on the economy, he said.

But the Bank was unlikely to cut currently high interest rates soon in view of the imminent easing of exchange controls on individuals and the continued high level of money supply and private sector credit growth.
"With the relaxation of exchange controls coming up, (Reserve Bank governor) Stals cannot afford to be lax in monetary policy," van Rensburg said.

On the recent confrontation between business and labour over controversial new labour legislation which this week sparked a one-day national strike, he said business had been negligent in not explaining choices to workers as clearly as possible:
"The choice is not between four months or six months maternity leave but between more jobs or less jobs...and having a job or not having a job," he said.
